client: I've been feeling really off ever since my grandmother passed away last month. It's like this heavy sadness that just won't lift, and I keep finding myself staring into space wondering what the point of everything is. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're carrying right now sounds genuinely heavy, and that persistent sadness and sense of emptiness makes complete sense given the depth of that grief. I notice that even as you're describing feeling lost and questioning the point of things, there's a part of you that reached out and said "I need to try something" — and that small but courageous step tells me something important about your resilience, even when it doesn't feel that way. Together, we can gently start to make sense of what you're experiencing, and I want you to know that talking *can* help, not by erasing the grief, but by helping you carry it a little differently.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure "resilient" is the right word for what I did — it felt more like desperation than courage, honestly. I've been sitting with this emptiness for weeks and I just didn't know what else to try. I guess I'm a little skeptical that talking about it will actually change how hollow everything feels right now.
therapist: It's really honest of you to push back on that — and actually, reframing it as desperation rather than courage isn't necessarily wrong, because sometimes desperation *is* what moves us forward when everything feels hollow, and that still took something. I'm also noticing that even as you're describing feeling empty and low, there's an energy in how you're expressing this — like part of you is actively wrestling with it rather than just resigned — and that tension is worth paying attention to. Your skepticism about whether talking will help is completely valid, and rather than trying to convince you otherwise, I'd gently invite you to just stay curious with me for now — not to "fix" the hollowness, but to understand what it's trying to tell you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess I can see what you mean about the energy thing, but honestly it feels more like agitation than anything meaningful. Like, I'm not wrestling with it in some hopeful way, I'm just... irritated that I don't know how to make it stop. And I'm not sure what the hollowness is "trying to tell me" — that framing almost makes it sound like there's some hidden wisdom in it, when it just feels like a void.
therapist: You're absolutely right to call that out — I was putting a frame on your experience that didn't fit, and I hear you that this isn't about hidden wisdom, it's just painful and frustrating and you want it to stop. The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of sharp edge to it — really matches what you're describing, that agitation of being stuck with something you can't solve. So let's be more straightforward together: what would it mean to you if the hollowness *did* start to lift, even just a little — what would feel different first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate that you backed off the reframing thing, that actually helps a little. If the hollowness started to lift, I think the first thing I'd notice is that I wouldn't dread Sunday evenings so much, that specific quiet when the week is ending and I'm just... alone with it all. Right now Sundays feel like this proof that nobody's really thinking about me, and if that changed even slightly, I think I'd feel less like I'm disappearing.
therapist: That image of Sunday evenings is really vivid and important — there's something about the way you described it, quietly and carefully, that tells me this isn't just a passing feeling but something you've sat with many times. I want to gently notice the thought underneath it: "nobody's really thinking about me" — that feels like a conclusion your mind has arrived at, and I'm curious what evidence you're drawing on to reach it, because grief can sometimes make that thought feel like a fact when it might be something worth examining. You said you'd feel "less like you're disappearing" if that changed — and I want you to know that right here, in this moment, I'm thinking about you, and what you've shared matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, I do... but it's hard not to feel like that's just your job, you know? Like, you're paid to think about me for this hour, and then when I walk out that door, I go right back to being someone nobody checks in on. The evidence feels pretty obvious to me — my phone doesn't ring, weekends pass without a single text, and I can't remember the last time someone reached out just to see how I was doing.
therapist: That's a completely fair thing to say, and I'm not going to argue with it — there's a real asymmetry in this relationship, and you deserve to name that. But I want to gently sit with the evidence you're describing, because I notice you're speaking quickly, with a kind of tightness in your voice, like this thought has been building pressure for a while — the silence from others feels like *proof* of your worth to them, but is it possible that people in grief sometimes pull back in ways that cause others to give space, not realizing that space feels like abandonment? I'm not dismissing the loneliness — it's clearly very real — but I wonder if "nobody checks in" and "nobody is thinking about me" are actually the same thing, or if grief might be making them feel identical right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically there's probably a difference between those two things. But when days go by and my phone stays silent, it just... it doesn't feel like a distinction that matters, you know? Like, even if they're thinking about me somewhere in their heads, I'm still sitting alone in my apartment, and that silence is what's real to me right now.
therapist: The way you just said that — softly, but quickly, like you've been holding it in — really lands, and I don't want to talk you out of it, because you're right that the silence in that apartment is *real* and it's what you're actually living inside. What you're describing is loneliness in a very concrete, physical sense, and that deserves to be acknowledged without me trying to reframe it away. I'm wondering though — during this past month, has there been even one small moment where you reached toward someone, or where connection felt even slightly possible, even if it didn't fully happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... there was one moment, I guess. My neighbor knocked on my door to ask if I had any extra coffee, and I ended up talking to her for maybe ten minutes in the doorway. But then I kind of pulled back and made an excuse to end it, and afterward I just felt this weird guilt, like I'd wasted her time or something.
therapist: That moment with your neighbor is actually really significant — you were present for it, even if only for ten minutes, and something in that exchange was real enough that you're still thinking about it. But I'm struck by what happened afterward: rather than feeling even a small sense of connection, your mind immediately went to "I wasted her time" — and I'm curious where that thought came from, because she knocked on *your* door, she stayed for ten minutes, and yet somehow you walked away carrying guilt instead of her. The way you described it just now, softly and a little quickly, like you're not sure it even counts — I wonder if that same thought, "I'm a burden, I'm wasting people's time," might be part of what's keeping you from reaching toward connection even when it's right there at your door.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, that hits something. I didn't even realize I was doing that until you just said it out loud like that. But I think part of me genuinely believes it — like, she was probably just being polite, and if I'd talked longer I would have confirmed what I already suspect, that I'm kind of... too much, or not enough, or something in between that's just exhausting to be around.
therapist: The way you just said that — high and fast, like the words were tumbling out before you could stop them — tells me this belief runs really deep, and I want to stay with it for a moment, because what you just named is important: "too much, or not enough, or something in between." That's an exhausting place to live, always pre-deciding that you'll be a burden before anyone else even gets the chance to respond. But I want to gently point out that your neighbor stayed for ten minutes in a doorway — she could have taken her coffee and left after thirty seconds, and she didn't.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying about the ten minutes, and part of me wants to hold onto that as evidence that maybe I'm not as much of a burden as I think. But then another part of me immediately jumps in and says she was just being polite, that she's a nice person and she would have stayed out of obligation, not because she actually wanted to be there. It's like I have this automatic reflex that takes any small good thing and finds a way to explain it away so it doesn't count.
therapist: What you just did right there is actually one of the most important things you've said today — you *named the reflex while it was happening*, which is different from just being caught in it. Your voice is moving fast and high, like your mind is racing to stay one step ahead of any hope before it can settle in, and that pattern you're describing — where good evidence gets automatically disqualified — is something we can actually work with directly in CBT, because it has a name and it's not the truth about you. I'm curious: if a close friend described their neighbor staying ten minutes in a doorway, would you help them explain it away, or would you let it count?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... no, I'd probably tell a friend that counts for something, that it shows the neighbor is trying. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm allowed to give other people the benefit of the doubt, but when I apply that same logic to myself it feels like I'm making excuses or letting myself off the hook too easily. I don't know why my brain works that way, but even right now I can feel myself wanting to argue against what you just said, which is kind of exhausting honestly.
therapist: The exhaustion in what you just said is real — your voice is soft but moving quickly, like even the act of recognizing this pattern takes effort, and I don't want to push past that tiredness. But what you've just discovered is genuinely significant: you already *have* the logic that would let this count, you use it freely for people you care about, and somewhere along the way you decided you don't qualify for that same compassion. That's not a character flaw — that's something grief and loneliness can do to a person, and it's also something we can gently, slowly start to change.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
